case_study_insert.main_stem: Zephyr Quay Fashion (ZQF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Zephyr, the business sells apparel through its own e-commerce site and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZQF plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and produces 72,000 units a year. ZQF faces two problems: its online return rate has climbed to 18% and picking errors are rising, while late deliveries are damaging customer ratings.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Operations Extract — Q4 2025: The online store fulfilled 18,400 orders last quarter, with a picking error rate of 2.1% and an online return rate of 18%, up from 13% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. Customer complaints rose from 46 to 71 per month. Market research of 500 online shoppers found that 68% value fast delivery and 57% would pay more for free returns. Returns-processing training for the 40 staff costs $650 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zephyr Quay Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.40 to $13.10 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale fabric and freight input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion grew 2.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: ZQF plans to fund part of its $720,000 fulfilment-centre expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZQF of using its $300,000 retained profit instead of that loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit costs ZQF no interest or capital repayments, so its cash flow is protected while it already carries $216,000 of fixed costs and an 18% return rate that ties up working capital. Every dollar not paid as loan interest stays inside the business to fund the picking-accuracy fixes needed after the 2.1% picking error rate and the rise in complaints from 46 to 71 a month. That protects the $7.00 contribution per unit earned on 72,000 units sold at $15.20 each, which is the cash the $720,000 expansion depends on.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If the new automated returns-processing centre fails to cut the 18% return rate, a lender could still demand repayment of the $420,000 bank loan, putting the jobs of the 40 staff and Nadia Zephyr's control at risk. Internal funding imposes no lender conditions and leaves the loan facility untouched as a reserve for a sudden spike in returns or the late-delivery problem. It also signals to staff that growth is being paid for out of trading success rather than debt, which supports morale in a flat structure where democratic leadership relies on trust.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZQF's financing, returns problem and contribution data.

questions.question_text: ZQF is launching a faster-delivery service for its online fashion range. Consider national television advertising, paid search advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should ZQF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would build mass awareness of the faster-delivery promise across the whole country, which could help ZQF win shoppers beyond its current customer base. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 40-person e-commerce business already funding a $720,000 expansion with a $420,000 loan, and much of the audience does not buy online fashion. Given that market research of 500 shoppers found 68% value fast delivery, a broad TV message would waste spend on the 32% who do not, and it cannot demonstrate the 3.8-day delivery claim credibly.

Paid search advertising: Buying search terms such as 'next-day fashion delivery' reaches shoppers at the moment they are ready to buy, and spend can be capped and measured against orders. It directly targets the 68% who value fast delivery and can be switched off if the 18% return rate makes sales unprofitable. Its weakness is that it only reaches people already searching, so it does little to build the brand or explain why ZQF's delivery is better, and competition for popular terms can push the cost per click up sharply.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion influencers can demonstrate the faster-delivery service and the new apparel range to a targeted audience, generating engagement and trust that a search advert cannot. It speaks directly to the 57% of surveyed shoppers who would pay more for better service, and it can show real parcels arriving in 3.8 days. The drawback is slower, less predictable volume and a dependence on influencer credibility, but cost per reached shopper is low and content can be reused across the site.

Recommendation: ZQF should choose paid search advertising as the primary launch channel, supported by a small influencer campaign. Search captures buyers at the point of purchase and is measurable against the 2.1% picking-error and return concerns; influencers supplement it with proof. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with $216,000 fixed costs and a $420,000 loan, and pure influencer marketing is rejected because its results are too slow to fill the new fulfilment centre.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies possible promotion channels with limited reference to ZQF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two channels with some application to ZQF's research and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three channels in the context of ZQF with a justified recommendation explaining why television and the weaker option are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZQF's online return rate has reached 18% and picking errors are rising. Explain two benefits for ZQF of using democratic leadership to improve performance in its fulfilment team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 40 warehouse and packing staff to help redesign picking routines, which gives them a voice in how the new returns-processing centre works. Because the people handling the orders know where the 2.1% picking errors occur, their suggestions can be more practical than top-down rules, and involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment under Maslow's social and esteem needs. Higher engagement should reduce the mistakes that feed the 18% return rate and help cut the 71 monthly complaints, protecting the $15.20 selling price and the $7.00 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Consulting the team makes the change to automated fulfilment easier to accept and lowers resistance and labour turnover. In a flat structure, staff who help set targets feel ownership of the $720,000 investment rather than fearing it, so they are more willing to learn the new returns workflow and to work to the 3.8-day delivery standard. That steadier attendance protects output of 72,000 units a year and makes the $650 per employee training spend more effective, since motivated workers apply what they learn. Democracy also surfaces problems early, letting managers fix defects before they reach customers and so defend the 57% of shoppers who value good service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZQF's returns, picking errors and flat structure.

questions.question_text: ZQF must improve picking accuracy among its 40 staff. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at a local college. Which should ZQF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the packing bench is directly relevant to ZQF's own picking routines and its new returns-processing centre, and it keeps all 40 staff productive while they learn, which protects the 18,400 orders fulfilled last quarter. The $650 per employee college fee is also avoided. Trainers are experienced packers, so the lessons target exactly the 2.1% picking errors and the 18% return rate. The drawbacks are that trainers' own output suffers, bad habits can be copied, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if large retail partners ask for proof of competence.

Off-the-job training: A local college course at $650 per employee would cost $26,000 for all 40 staff, affordable beside the $720,000 expansion. It gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification, and takes workers away from the noise of the fulfilment centre so they can focus on accuracy and returns handling. However, it removes staff from the line, reducing capacity while the 3.8-day delivery promise must be kept, and the generic content may not match ZQF's exact scanning system, so follow-up coaching on site would still be required.

Decision: ZQF should choose on-the-job training for all 40 staff, with short college top-ups for the senior pickers. It is machine-and-process specific, avoids losing output at a time when complaints have risen from 46 to 71 a month, and spends nothing on the $650 fee. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing the whole team would endanger 72,000-unit output and the delivery promise, and the $26,000 fee is better reserved for the automated centre; the certificate gap can be closed later by sending a few supervisors to college.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ZQF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of ZQF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the 2.1% picking errors.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZQF's management can use its cost and break-even data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,857.14 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 72,000-unit output; pricing/free-returns modelling against $216,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.20 to attack the 18% return rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($15.20 − $8.20) = $216,000 ÷ $7.00 = 30,857.14 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,857.14 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.20 − $8.20 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZQF's management can use this cost data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,857.14-unit break-even point with output of 72,000 units, giving a margin of safety of about 41,143 units, to see how far sales can fall before the new fulfilment centre loses money.
2. Use the $7.00 contribution per unit to model the cost of offering free returns: each refunded order destroys that contribution, so the 18% return rate can be priced into the $15.20 selling price.
3. Check that contribution on 72,000 units covers $216,000 fixed costs and leaves cash for interest on the $420,000 loan, testing whether the $720,000 expansion is affordable.
4. Benchmark unit cost of $11.20 ($216,000 ÷ 72,000 + $8.20) each quarter to spot waste from picking errors and to judge whether the 2.1% error rate is being reduced.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZQF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZQF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.45 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.54 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.98 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.01 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $290,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $165,000 + $48,000 = $323,000. Current assets 2024 divided by $200,000 current liabilities = 1.45; 2025 divided by $210,000 = 1.54. Liquid assets 2024 = ($290,000 − $95,000) = $195,000, divided by $200,000 = 0.98; 2025 = ($323,000 − $110,000) = $213,000, divided by $210,000 = 1.01.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The first ratio rose from 1.45 to 1.54 as current assets grew from $290,000 to $323,000, helped by trade receivables climbing from $140,000 to $165,000. More importantly, the second measure, which strips out inventories, rose from 0.98 to 1.01, so ZQF is no longer depending on selling stock to meet its $210,000 short-term obligations. That matters while it commits $420,000 to a bank loan and $720,000 to the fulfilment centre, and while an 18% return rate already ties up cash. Cash did fall from $55,000 to $48,000 and receivables are rising, so if online shoppers or payment platforms pay late the improvement could reverse quickly; the 57% of shoppers wanting free returns may also force more cash into refunds.

Conclusion: ZQF's financial position has improved. Both measures rose, and the rise in the second one shows the gain is not merely a stock build-up. The residual risk is the $165,000 of receivables and lower cash, so tighter credit control should accompany the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether ZQF's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZQF of offering free online returns as part of its $720,000 expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free returns directly answer the market research in which 57% of 500 online shoppers said they would pay more for that service, and they can help ZQF tackle an 18% return rate that is currently driven by a 2.1% picking error rate. A generous returns policy reduces the perceived risk of buying apparel online, so it can lift orders from the 18,400 processed last quarter and defend the $15.20 selling price and $7.00 contribution per unit. It also supports the 68% of shoppers who value fast delivery, strengthening the launch of the new fulfilment centre and encouraging repeat purchases.

Disadvantage: Free returns are expensive because each refunded order destroys the $7.00 contribution and leaves ZQF with the $8.20 variable cost and the outbound delivery cost unrecovered. With returns already at 18%, the policy could push costs well above the $216,000 fixed costs and make the $420,000 loan harder to service. It may also encourage over-ordering and more 71-a-month complaints if the 3.8-day delivery time slips, and the packing hub must handle reversed goods, adding work for the 40 staff just as the automated centre is bedded in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZQF's research, return rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in fabric and freight input costs will affect ZQF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If ZQF's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside $216,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the immediate effect is zero. Higher rates may still make consumers more cautious about online fashion spending, which grew only 2.4%, and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $720,000 centre. ZQF can reduce this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.10 per hour): With a workforce of 40, most packing and returns roles are likely hourly paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is productivity: 72,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,800 units per worker. If output per worker holds or rises, the higher wage is affordable; if the 18% return rate and 2.1% picking errors push rework up, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.6% fabric and freight): ZQF's variable cost of $8.20 a unit covers goods and delivery, but the insert does not break it down. An illustrative upper bound assumes the whole $8.20 is exposed: 9.6% × $8.20 = $0.79 a unit, which at 72,000 units is about $56,700 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution from $7.00 toward $6.20, directly weakening the cash flow available for the $420,000 loan and the $720,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It compounds across every unit and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that justifies the investment, whereas the interest rise is conditional and small at $3,150 and the wage rise can be offset by the 1,800-unit productivity if returns are controlled.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZQF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ZQF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
